Promethium
Marinsky, Glendenin, Coryell
United States
From Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire from the gods.
After many false claims (including «florentium» from Florence), it was identified with certainty in 1945 among the fission products of uranium at the Oak Ridge laboratory.
In nature there are only minute traces; it is produced in nuclear reactors.
Luminous paints, nuclear batteries for pacemakers and space probes, thickness gauges.
It is the only rare earth with no stable isotopes.
Samarium
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran
France
From the mineral samarskite, named after the Russian engineer Samarsky: the first element named (indirectly) after a person.
Lecoq de Boisbaudran identified it in 1879 with the spectroscope.
It is extracted from monazite and bastnäsite.
Heat-resistant samarium-cobalt magnets, electric guitars, medicines for bone pain, nuclear reactors.
Samarium magnets keep working even at very high temperatures, where neodymium magnets give up.
Europium
Eugène-Anatole Demarçay
France
From Europe.
Demarçay separated it from samarium in 1901 after years of repeated crystallisations.
It is among the least abundant rare earths; it is extracted from bastnäsite.
Red and blue phosphors for screens and fluorescent lamps, banknote security.
Euro banknotes have europium inks that glow under ultraviolet light: an element named after Europe that protects the euro!
Gadolinium
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac
Switzerland
After the Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin, a pioneer of rare-earth research.
Marignac observed it in 1880; Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated it in 1886.
It is extracted from monazite and bastnäsite.
Contrast agent for MRI scans, nuclear control rods, X-ray screens, magnetic refrigeration.
It becomes magnetic only when it is cold: below about 20 °C a magnet attracts it, above that it does not.
Terbium
Carl Gustaf Mosander
Sweden
From the village of Ytterby.
Mosander separated it from yttrium in 1843, together with erbium.
It is extracted from the ionic clays of southern China.
Green phosphors for screens and lamps, magnets for electric cars, sonar, printer heads.
The alloy Terfenol-D changes shape in a magnetic field: with it you can make a table «sing» like a loudspeaker.
Dysprosium
Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran
France
From the Greek dysprositos, «hard to get».
Lecoq de Boisbaudran needed 32 attempts to separate it from holmium oxide in 1886, working on his kitchen table.
It is extracted from the ionic clays of China.
Magnets for electric cars and wind turbines, nuclear control rods, lasers.
Its name means «hard to get»: and in fact it was isolated in pure form only in the 1950s.
Holmium
Marc Delafontaine, Jacques-Louis Soret; Per Teodor Cleve
Switzerland / Sweden
From Holmia, the Latin name of Stockholm.
It was observed with the spectroscope in Geneva in 1878 and isolated independently by Cleve in Sweden in 1879.
It is extracted from monazite and gadolinite.
Surgical and dental lasers, very strong magnets, calibration of spectrophotometers.
It has the highest magnetic moment of all naturally occurring elements.
Erbium
Carl Gustaf Mosander
Sweden
From the village of Ytterby.
Mosander found it in 1843 in the mineral gadolinite from Ytterby.
It is extracted from ionic clays and xenotime.
Amplifiers for internet optical fibres, lasers for dermatology, pink glass and jewellery.
The internet travels thousands of kilometres through optical fibres thanks, in part, to tiny amounts of erbium that amplify the light.
Thulium
Per Teodor Cleve
Sweden
From Thule, the ancient name of a mythical northern land.
Cleve discovered it in 1879 by separating it from erbium oxide.
It is one of the rarest rare earths; it is extracted from monazite.
Portable X-ray devices, medical lasers, banknote security.
It is so rare that it has very few uses: it costs as much as some precious metals.
Ytterbium
Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac
Switzerland
From the village of Ytterby.
Marignac separated it from erbium in 1878; it was later found to contain lutetium as well.
It is extracted from monazite and xenotime.
Experimental atomic clocks among the most precise in the world, lasers, stainless steel.
Ytterbium clocks are so precise that they would lose one second in billions of years.
Lutetium
Georges Urbain; Carl Auer von Welsbach
France / Austria
From Lutetia, the Latin name of Paris.
It was separated from ytterbium in 1907 at the same time by Urbain in Paris and by Auer von Welsbach in Austria, who argued about the name for a long time.
It is the most expensive rare earth; it is extracted from monazite and xenotime.
PET scanners, cancer therapies (lutetium-177), catalysts.
Lutetium-177 is used as a radioactive «missile» that hits tumour cells.
Hafnium
Dirk Coster, George de Hevesy
Denmark
From Hafnia, the Latin name of Copenhagen.
Bohr predicted that element 72 should resemble zirconium; Coster and Hevesy found it in zirconium minerals in Copenhagen in 1923.
It is always obtained together with zirconium, to which it is almost identical.
Control rods in nuclear reactors, superalloys, modern microchips.
Zirconium and hafnium are so similar that nature has always kept them together: that is why nobody had noticed it before.
Tantalum
Anders Gustaf Ekeberg
Sweden
From Tantalus, a figure of Greek mythology, because its oxide never gets «filled» with acid.
Ekeberg discovered it in 1802; for decades it was confused with niobium.
It is extracted from coltan, mostly in Congo and Rwanda.
Capacitors for phones and computers, prostheses, surgical instruments, turbine blades.
Almost every smartphone contains a little tantalum in its tiny capacitors.
Tungsten
Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar
Spain
From the Swedish tung sten, «heavy stone». The symbol W comes from wolfram.
The Elhuyar brothers isolated it in 1783 from wolframite.
It is extracted from wolframite and scheelite, mostly in China.
Light-bulb filaments, tungsten-carbide tools, drill bits, counterweights, welding electrodes.
It has the highest melting point of all metals: 3,422 °C.
Rhenium
Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, Otto Berg
Germany
From the river Rhine (Rhenus in Latin).
It was the last stable element to be discovered, in 1925, searched for with X-rays in platinum and columbite ores.
It is one of the rarest elements; it is obtained from molybdenum and copper ores (Chile, United States).
Superalloys for jet engines, catalysts for high-octane petrol.
It was the last stable element to be discovered: all the ones found later are radioactive.
Osmium
Smithson Tennant
England
From the Greek osme, «smell», for the strong smell of its oxide.
Tennant discovered it in 1803 in the black residue left after dissolving platinum in aqua regia.
It is obtained from platinum ores.
Fountain-pen nibs, electrical contacts, precision instruments.
It is the densest element of all: a 10 cm cube would weigh more than 22 kilograms.
Iridium
Smithson Tennant
England
From Iris, goddess of the rainbow, for the varied colours of its salts.
Tennant found it in 1803 together with osmium in platinum residues.
It is obtained from platinum ores; it is more common in meteorites.
Spark plugs, crucibles, electrical contacts; the old standard metre and kilogram were made of platinum-iridium.
A layer rich in iridium in 66-million-year-old rocks (also studied at Gubbio, in Italy) points to the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs.
Platinum
Antonio de Ulloa
Spain (South America)
From the Spanish platina, «little silver».
It was used by pre-Columbian peoples of Ecuador. The Spanish navigator de Ulloa described it in 1735 in Colombia.
It is mined mostly in South Africa and Russia.
Catalytic converters, jewellery, electrodes, anti-cancer drugs (cisplatin), precision thermometers.
The Spanish conquistadors threw it into rivers, thinking it was «unripe» silver.
Gold
Known since prehistory
From the Old English gold; the symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum, «shining dawn».
It was among the first metals used by humans, because it is found pure in nature. The oldest gold jewellery is over 6,000 years old.
It is mined in China, Australia, Russia, Canada and the United States; it is also found as nuggets in rivers.
Jewellery, bank reserves, electronics, dentistry, astronauts' visors.
With just one gram of gold you can draw a wire more than 2 kilometres long.
Mercury
Known since antiquity
From the god Mercury, as quick as this flowing metal. The symbol Hg comes from hydrargyrum, «liquid silver».
It was known to the Chinese, Indians and Egyptians. The mines of Almadén in Spain and of Monte Amiata in Tuscany were among the most important.
It is extracted from cinnabar, a red mineral.
Thermometers and barometers (now banned), fluorescent lamps, gold mining, dental amalgams.
It is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. The first emperor of China may have died drinking mercury potions.
Thallium
William Crookes
England
From the Greek thallos, «green shoot», for the green line in its spectrum.
Crookes discovered it in 1861 with the spectroscope in the residues of a sulfuric-acid factory.
It is obtained as a by-product of zinc and lead.
Nuclear medicine (heart scans), electronics, special glasses.
It was called «the poisoner's poison» because it has no taste and no smell. Agatha Christie used it in one of her novels.
Lead
Known since antiquity
From the Old English lead; the symbol Pb comes from the Latin plumbum, which also gave us the word «plumber».
The Romans used it for their water pipes. It is one of the oldest metals worked by humans.
It is extracted from galena (China, Australia, Peru) and widely recycled from batteries.
Car batteries, shielding against X-rays, ballast, lead crystal.
Lead is the end point of three great radioactive decay chains: uranium and thorium become lead after billions of years.
Bismuth
Claude François Geoffroy
France
From the German Wismut, possibly «white mass».
It was known in the Middle Ages but confused with tin and lead. Geoffroy showed in 1753 that it was a separate element.
It is obtained as a by-product of lead, copper and tungsten, mostly in China.
Stomach medicines, pearly cosmetics, low-melting alloys for fire sprinklers, lead substitute.
Its crystals look like rainbow staircases. For a long time it was thought to be stable, but in 2003 it was found to decay over billions of billions of years.
Polonium
Marie and Pierre Curie
France
From Poland, Marie Curie's homeland.
The Curies discovered it in 1898 by processing tonnes of pitchblende, because it was much more radioactive than the uranium it contained.
Traces occur in uranium ores; it is produced in reactors.
Anti-static brushes, heat sources for satellites, research.
Marie Curie named it to draw attention to Poland, which at the time did not exist as an independent country.
Astatine
Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie, Emilio Segrè
United States
From the Greek astatos, «unstable».
It was produced in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles. Emilio Segrè was again among the discoverers.
It is the rarest naturally occurring element: the whole Earth's crust contains less than 30 grams at any moment.
Research on cancer therapies with astatine-211.
Nobody has ever seen a piece of astatine: if you gathered enough, it would vaporise from the heat of its own radioactivity.
Radon
Ernest Rutherford, Robert Owens; Friedrich Ernst Dorn
Canada / Germany
From radium, the element it forms from.
Rutherford and Owens noticed in 1899 a radioactive gas given off by thorium; Dorn found it in 1900 given off by radium.
It forms continuously in the ground from the decay of uranium and collects in cellars and on lower floors.
Earthquake research, geological studies; in the past it was used in radiotherapy.
It is invisible and odourless: that is why radon is measured in homes, especially in areas of volcanic rock such as Lazio, around Rome.
Francium
Marguerite Perey
France
From France.
Marguerite Perey, an assistant at the Curie Institute, discovered it in 1939 while studying the decay of actinium.
There is very little in nature: it forms from the decay of actinium and disappears within minutes.
Scientific research only.
Its longest-lived isotope lasts just 22 minutes. Perey was the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences.
Radium
Marie and Pierre Curie
France
From the Latin radius, «ray».
The Curies discovered it in 1898; Marie isolated it as a metal in 1910 after processing tonnes of pitchblende. It earned her a second Nobel Prize.
It occurs in traces in uranium ores.
In the past, luminous paints for watches; today medicines against bone tumours (radium-223).
It glows in the dark with a bluish light. Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive and are consulted with gloves and protection.
Actinium
André-Louis Debierne
France
From the Greek aktinos, «ray».
Debierne, a friend of the Curies, found it in 1899 in pitchblende residues.
It occurs in traces in uranium ores.
Neutron sources, cancer therapies (actinium-225).
It gives its name to the actinide family. It glows in the dark with a blue light.
Thorium
Jöns Jacob Berzelius
Sweden
From Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
Berzelius discovered it in 1829 in a black Norwegian mineral later called thorite.
It is three times more abundant than uranium; it occurs in monazite (India, Brazil, Australia).
Mantles of old gas lamps, welding electrodes, a possible nuclear fuel of the future.
Much of the Earth's internal heat comes from the decay of thorium and uranium.
